meta.title: Who really said "I declare to you that woman must not depend upon the protection of man"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Susan B. Anthony really said it — sourced to her July 1871 San Francisco speech. The documented wording is trimmer than the version quote sites circulate.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I declare to you that woman must not depend upon the protection of man'?
meta.ogDescription: Yes, Susan B. Anthony. Wikiquote sources the line to her July 1871 San Francisco speech; the fuller 'and there I take my stand' form circulates unsourced.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Anthony spoke this during her 1871 lecture tour of the Pacific Coast. Wikiquote’s sourced section ties the line to her “Speech in San Francisco (July 1871),” where the documented wording runs “Woman must not depend upon the protection of man, but must be taught to protect herself.” The widely circulated fuller form — “I declare to you … and there I take my stand” — adds a rhetorical preface and coda but preserves the same statement.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: I declare to you that woman must not depend upon the protection of man, but must be taught to protect herself, and there I take my stand.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Sourced section as coming from Anthony’s “Speech in San Francisco (July 1871),” not among its misattributed or disputed entries.
Quote aggregators such as Goodreads circulate the fuller “I declare to you … and there I take my stand” wording but attach no primary source.
The sentiment matches Anthony’s documented 1871 Pacific Coast lectures on women’s independence, recounted in Ida Husted Harper’s Life and Work of Susan B. Anthony.
source.excerptNote: The wording documented in Wikiquote’s sourced section is the trimmer “Woman must not depend upon the protection of man, but must be taught to protect herself”; the “I declare to you … and there I take my stand” frame is how the line is most often reproduced.
source.rightsNote: The line was spoken and reported in 1871 and is long in the public domain in the United States; Anthony died in 1906, and no 1931-or-later edition or translation governs this English-language text.

author.name: Susan B. Anthony
author.heading: About Susan B. Anthony
author.bio: Susan Brownell Anthony was a leading American suffragist and social reformer who, with Elizabeth Cady Stanton, founded the National Woman Suffrage Association and campaigned for decades for women’s right to vote and for women’s economic and legal independence. In 1872 she was arrested, tried, and fined for casting a ballot in the presidential election. She did not live to see the Nineteenth Amendment (1920), often called the “Anthony Amendment,” which secured women’s suffrage nationally.

misattribution.heading: A note on wording
misattribution.intro: This one is correctly credited — the issue is wording, not authorship. The version that spreads online is a fuller rendering than the form documented from Anthony’s speech.

items.why: circulate “I declare to you … and there I take my stand” with no citation, while the sourced form recorded in Wikiquote is the shorter “Woman must not depend upon the protection of man, but must be taught to protect herself.”

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the words are genuinely Anthony’s, tied to her July 1871 San Francisco speech — Wikiquote, sourced section.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Self-reliance was the spine of Anthony’s argument for suffrage: she held that women’s subordination flowed from economic and legal dependence on men, and that the ballot — not male chivalry — was the real guarantee of a woman’s safety and standing. This line, delivered on her 1871 Pacific Coast tour, compresses that whole case into a single declaration.

Its endurance on posters, mugs, and social feeds comes from that portability: it reads as a crisp mission statement for independence, which is also why it now circulates in a punchier, source-stripped form.
